As many particles as this GPU can draw smoothly
Measured just now: {n, number}

As many particles as this GPU can draw smoothly
Measured as the world starts
gloss.light: Producers feed on light. The light level in the pool varies with the era and is brightest inside tide bands, most of all at the height of the season.
gloss.era: Every 10–18 minutes the climate turns: the baseline light and the water’s temperature change, one tide wave is replaced, and the currents shift. In about one era in six the water stands low and the highest ground shows as islands of dry land.
gloss.maps: One map over the view at a time. Light colors every point by the light a photosynthesizing cell would get there; Heat is a thermal camera, deep blue to teal to amber to white over a span from 2° below the background water to 10° above it, with a contour line every 2°; Tide shows the light the Tide brings and where its bands are heading. Its key (G, E, H) or gauge opens it, and again closes it.
gloss.haze: Warm water bends light like the air over a hot road. Off, the view holds still over warm water (boiling water still roils). Auto draws it, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late.
gloss.thermal: How well a cell works at its temperature: a rate that scales its photosynthesis, digestion, and swimming. It is at its best within a narrow tolerance of the species’ optimum. Away from its optimum a cell also pays extra upkeep for the stress.
gloss.optimum: The temperature a species works best at (0–45°). It drifts by mutation, so lineages can follow the climate or find a warm or cold refuge. A spark of life creates a species suited to the water it sparked in.
gloss.heatmaker: A species that burns extra energy (up to 0.03 per second) as heat. Its cells run warmer than the water, more so in a body, and its colonies warm the water around them. They can serve as lifeboats for warmth-lovers in a cold snap, but they may easily overheat in a heatwave.
gloss.torpor: Far below its optimum temperature (more than 1.25 tolerances) a cell goes torpid: it doesn't feed, swim, or divide. Torpid cells pay a quarter of their upkeep, dim in color, stop pulsing, and fall silent until the water warms again.
gloss.evdrought: A drought: the water falls over several minutes until a third to two thirds of the floor lies dry, parting the pool into separate pools. Cells stranded on the mud shrivel; most rest as cysts. After a while, rain refills it, cold, and dim. Then, the cysts that survived wake.
gloss.heatwave: A deviation of the climate: for a few minutes the water’s background temperature rises (a heat wave) or falls (a cold snap) by 5–8°.
gloss.diet: The share of energy a species takes from each type of food. Food is worth its energy × share × 1.5. Partly photosynthetic species get less from food.
gloss.cyst: A dormant cell. An animal cell running out of energy with nothing to eat in reach may go dormant. It stops swimming and pulsing, turns gray, leaks only a little energy, and wakes at random, after about 45 seconds on average. Nothing can eat a cyst. Cysts are the seed bank that carries a lineage through hard times.
gloss.satiety: A hunter attacks animals less the fuller it gets. Once a hunter holds more energy than it needs to divide, it rests instead of killing.
gloss.stone: Sand, and the skeletons of calcifying cells. Stone never drifts and the living cannot pass through it. Attacks made from among stone sometimes miss, so prey shelters in reefs, and calcifying cells settle on their own reef while everything else must go around it. Sand in the pool at the start of a world lasts nearly an hour. A loose grain of reef stone crumbles within minutes and a tightly packed one lasts far longer, but a reef that spreads to fill most of the area around it wears away fast. So reefs stay as separate patches.
gloss.saves: A save records the whole world: every particle, each species with its name and lineage, the chronicle, the history, and the climate’s eras. Saves live in this browser’s storage, which clearing site data erases; download one to keep it safe or to open it on another device.
gloss.adapting: The simulation may reduce render quality if it is unable to maintain full quality at a smooth frame rate. This describes the reason: frames running late, the GPU busy for nearly the whole frame, the device under pressure (hot or busy, where the browser reports it), or the browser’s own pace (it hands out frames more slowly than the screen refreshes while the page has little to do: only the frame rate is lowered then). With Target fps on Auto it lowers the frame rate to 30 first, then eases what Adaptation may (work done less often, effects, the render scale), and below 30 only once nothing else is left. Adaptation will gradually restore quality if conditions improve, returning to 60 fps last.
gloss.drawms: GPU time drawing the world once takes: cells, stone, bloom, and the final image.
gloss.stride: How much simulated time each step moves the world forward. Normally a step is 1/60 s, the most exact. At higher simulation speeds when the GPU can’t keep up, it takes bigger strides per step instead, up to 6/60 s. A device that runs the world at 30 fps needs to double the stride to keep the same speed (2/60 s). Bigger steps are a little coarser and interpolate cell actions, but births, deaths, and the variety of species stay roughly the same over long runs.
gloss.mind-matter: The pull or push of silt, husks, and stone on its receptors (apart from appetite). Stone solidly pushes on any non-calcifying cell.
gloss.mind-flee: Flight: an animal that is not a hunter swims away from hunters near it. It swims harder the closer they get, up to the limit of its swimming ability.
gloss.film: Records the view as a video, with the auto camera’s captions and the soundtrack, until you stop it (R, or Stop on the red strip). On devices that support it, the film is written to disk as it is recorded. It stops itself before it grows too big (up to 8 GB, or an hour or more at 1080p).
gloss.autoidle: Left alone for a minute (three with a panel open), the camera starts exploring the world on its own. Drag, scroll, or tap to take it back.
gloss.icescale: The resolution the ice is drawn at: Full, or Half. Auto draws it in full, and Adaptation may halve it while frames run late. Setting to Full or Half disables auto adaptation.
gloss.seaevery: How often the water’s waves are calculated: every frame (Full), every second frame, or every fourth. Setting this to less often should save some performance and only show a little less motion in the light. Auto Adaptation may lower this setting while frames run late. Setting this to a value other than Auto will disable the auto adaption for this setting. Display → Surface sets how strong the waves are.
gloss.contactsevery: To save performance, this setting can reduce the portion of cells which are checked each frame to determine how many other cells are touching. This is used to draw cells pressed together into tissue. For cells that aren't checked in a frame, the contacts calculated from before are carried along, a few frames old at most. Auto looks at half each frame, and Adaptation may take it to a quarter while frames run late. Setting this to Half or Quarter disables auto adaptation.
gloss.stoneevery: How often the light on stone is worked out again while the world runs: every half second, every second, or every two. Stone changes slowly, so it doesn't need to be updated every frame. Auto relights it every half second, and Adaptation may relight it less often while frames run late. Setting this to anything other than Auto will disable adaptation.
gloss.splitsteps: At 60 fps, if a step of the world does not fit in a frame beside drawing, Auto takes steps of two sixtieths of a second and spreads each over two frames: the view keeps 60 fps and moves on every frame. Auto does this only where it is needed. Off never splits a step.
gloss.adapt: When On, frames running late will retarget the simulation to 30 fps instead of 60, then eases individual settings which this device performs worst with: work done less often (the water’s waves, cells’ contacts, the stone’s light), the heat haze, the suspension, and only then the microscope, cells’ insides, more resolution and, last, the glow. With room it brings them back the other way, up to 60 fps. It eases only the settings left on Auto, in Display and under Pacing. Settings auto adapted are listed here; a value you choose stays as chosen. Off, everything is drawn in full (render scale and frame rate still follow their own settings).
gloss.density: The most device pixels drawn per CSS pixel. High-density (Retina) screens look sharper at 2× but cost up to four times the pixels of 1×. Auto draws at 1× (up to 1.5× while filming). 1× is recommended for most devices.
gloss.targetfps: Frames per second that the system is aiming for, as a whole number of the screen’s refreshes so frames stay evenly spaced. 30 FPS halves the GPU’s work and saves battery; Display follows the screen’s refresh rate. Simulated time keeps pace with real time at any rate. Auto aims for 60 and, when the device can’t keep up, drops to 30 before easing anything else. Choose a rate other than Auto to lock the target to that rate.
gloss.bloom: A soft glow around bright cells. The microscope’s warm halation and the lamp’s veiling flare. Requires several extra full-screen passes. Auto draws it, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late.
gloss.lod: Zoomed in, cells resolve into membranes, organelles and fused bodies; bonds resolve into soft bending strands. Off, every cell stays the glowing point it is from afar, at any zoom. This is far cheaper, so the simulation can run more particles. This setting does not affect the species cards portraits. Auto draws zoom detail until Adaptation decides to leave them out while frames run late.
gloss.specks: The fine suspension that drifts between cells when zoomed far in. Off saves a compute pass and a full-screen pass. Auto draws it, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late.
gloss.particles: Particles include every stone grain, husk, and cell. Their number is fixed for a world’s whole duration and can't be changed without resetting the world. Auto measures the GPU and picks the most it can run smoothly. Changing the setting requires starting a new world.
gloss.neighbors: The most nearby particles a cell weighs each step. Cells only pick food and bond partners from those it saw. The cells it touches (bodies parting, a crowd’s drag) are sampled in proportion to this setting. Fewer neighbors runs faster in dense colonies and makes no difference in open water. Auto weighs 112 and gives up to 88 or 64 only on a device where the step costs a lot. Changing it takes effect at once.
gloss.scale: Lengths are in micrometers (µm, a thousandth of a millimeter). Cells of ordinary size are about 10 µm across, about the size of a protist. A cell senses and pulls on others at most about 60 µm away.
gloss.song: Every species has its own song, read from its genome. Its surface signature picks the notes, how it lives sets the rhythm, tempo and range (hunters leap in quick clipped figures, drifting producers sway through long ones), and its color picks the instrument. A mutant sings a variation: a few notes moved, or the tune turned upside down, reversed or answered. Its cells sing if they are in view of the camera, in step if the species schools; a bonded colony adds a second voice.
gloss.sigil: The species’ sigil is drawn from the species' song: one cell per note, in the shape and color of the cell type that sings it, as large as the note is long and turned by its pitch, packed in the order they sing as a colony grows. Cells in the sigil are linked only if the species bonds.
gloss.instrument: The instrument a species sings with. Picked by how its family lives (hunter, grazer, producer scavenger). Its exact voice and timbre is determined by its color.
gloss.register: How high the species sings. Free-floating producers and scavengers sing high, hunters low.
gloss.watersurface: The surface of the water far above the cells, out of focus: as its waves pass they gently bend the view. The passing bands of light highlight the crests of the waves. Waves get more intense during a storm. Subtle tones it down, Strong turns it up, Off holds the water still. Auto sets it to Normal, and Adaptation may calculate the waves less often, or turn it off when frames run late.
gloss.microlook: Post-processing effects that give the appearance of a darkfield microscope: black water, outlines glowing as light catches their edges and touched with rainbow, a soft focus away from the middle and a little grain, seen through the eyepiece’s lens (colors parting toward the edges, a round field stop darkening the corners, dust drifting out of focus). Subtle tones it down, Strong turns it up, Off shows the cells plainly, without the lens. Auto sets it to Normal, and Adaptation may turn it off while frames run late. The O key turns it off and back on.
gloss.filmgrain: A fine flicker of grain over the picture, as on film, strongest in the midtones. Fine is barely seen, Heavy looks like an old reel; Off disables all film grain.
gloss.audiomusic: The composed music under everything: the piano, strings, and vibraphone that follow the era and the species that reign. Off leaves only the life and the water.
gloss.audiocells: The cells themselves: every species singing its own short song, births ringing, bites, and deaths. From afar, the murmur of the crowd. Off leaves the music and the water.
gloss.audiowater: The water's sound: the sea’s low hum, the drone under the harmony, and the waves that wash in now and then. Off is a dry, close room.
gloss.annotations: Live notes drawn over the world on what is happening in view: who is hunting or grazing on whom, a species scalding in water, cells stilled by the cold, a new species budding off, etc. They can be displayed only when the auto camera is on (default), always, or never.
gloss.diversity: How many species the world effectively has, counting each by how common it is, so rare species count for less. Ten equally common species score 10; ten where one holds nearly every cell score under 2. The exponential of the Shannon entropy of species populations.
gloss.will: The viewer’s will, imparted on this cell while it is ridden. It is one more drive amongst the cells other drives, but the viewer's will is strong. The cell is compelled toward where it is steered, as strong as its swimming skill allows.
gloss.ride: Ride this cell (or just press W A S D or an arrow key with it selected): the camera dives to it and follows it, and W A S D, the arrow keys or a held click or finger steer it. This compels the cell to move in the willed direction as one more strong drive among its other drives. It moves as fast as its genes allow: held, it gathers speed over a second or so; tapped, it edges foward. Tab goes to its newest child. If it dies as one cell of a body, the ride automatically switches to another cell in the body. If it dies alone, the ride ends and Enter rides a kin. Enter, Esc or a click on another cell stops riding.
gloss.toolreach: How far every tool but the needle reaches. This sets the effect radius for all tools and is displayed by the ring around the pointer. [ ] or ⇧ wheel also change it.
guide.overview.p1: Tidemote is a sealed world on the surface of a torus: what leaves one edge enters the opposite one. Every point in the world is a particle in the water. The total number of particles never changes, they only change form: inert <silt>silt</silt>, living cells, dead <husk>husks</husk>, and <stone>stone</stone>: the world's bedrock and the reefs that calcifying cells leave behind.
guide.overview.p2: Energy is the only thing that enters and leaves. The first kind of energy is the <light>light</light>: the pool of water receives a different amount of background light every era, and is brightest in the bands of the <tide>Tide</tide>. The second kind of energy is heat: emitted by oxidizing <framboid>framboids</framboid>, rotting husks, and by the energy cells spend on <upkeep>upkeep</upkeep> which warms the <water>water</water>, spreads, drifts on the currents and is lost to the deep. Everything you see grows out of a handful of local rules applied to every particle many times a second.
guide.cycle.feeding: Feeding. Photosynthetic cells drink light; others eat plants a bite at a time, husks, or other cells (flesh), according to their diet. A killed cell becomes a husk, an eaten husks turn into silt, and what an eater cannot digest it drops as dung, another form of husk. Cells stop feeding once they have enough energy to divide.
guide.cycle.mutation: Mutation. Each division has a small chance of founding a new species with a slightly different genome.
guide.cycle.death: Death. At zero energy (starvation) or at the end of its lifespan a cell becomes a husk carrying leftover energy. Husks eventually decay and crumble into silt. A settled calcifying cell may leave stone instead, usually beside stone already there; which forms solid reefs in the water. Stone eventually wears back into silt over a few minutes.
guide.cycle.dormancy: Dormancy. An animal running out of energy with no food in reach may go dormant as a cyst, a low energy state, to bide time until they can wake later.
guide.climate.p1: The <tide>Tide</tide> is four slow waves summed over the torus; where they add up, bright bands form and drift. Inside a band it is bright; outside, it is dim but never dark. What lies in a band is lit bright, the murk beneath it glows and the silt in the waves' crests sparkle, while what lies outside is dim and cool. <light>Light</light> is what plant cells feed on: plants crowded together share it, so meadows bloom under a passing band and thin out behind it, and the rest of the lifecycle follows.
guide.climate.p2: The <season>season</season> is a 5-minute cycle that swings tide strength between 10% and 100%. This is the Tide percentage shown in the gauge and graphs. The bands keep their shape; only the strength of light in them changes. At high tide they are bright and the water is a little warmer. At low tide they fade until they are barely brighter than the rest of the world. This drives the regular booms and busts. Every 10–18 minutes a new <era>era</era> begins: the baseline light changes, one tide wave is replaced so the bright zones form and move differently, and two water current patterns are swapped. The water’s temperature walks from era to era, so each world has its own thermal history. Eras are usually named after the differences they bring to the world: water warming or cooling, light rising or failing, the water falling to reveal the floor or rising over it again, storm events, drought events, frost events, duckweed events, or the life that holds the pool (a bloom, a dwindling, hunters or grazers gaining, a genus reigning, a burst of new species). The event log records precisely what changes with each era.
guide.climate.p3: Tap a gauge to display its data as map over the view: Light opens the light map, Temp the thermal camera, and Tide the tide map (on phones, tap the era name).
guide.climate.p4: Settings → Map → Light colors every point by the light a photosynthesizing cell would receive there, with a contour every 10%; Settings → Currents draws the flow that carries silt and drifting cells. The Tide gauge at the top follows the season: the dot rides the 5-minute wave, and the Temp thermometer beside it shows the background temperature, with an arrow while it changes; it blinks during a heat wave or cold snap.
guide.heat.p1: The water has a temperature, and most of its warmth comes from life. Every unit of energy a cell spends on <upkeep>upkeep</upkeep> becomes heat in its water, so crowds, bodies, and reefs sit in warm patches of their own making. A little heat also comes from sunlight, from rotting carcass piles, and from <framboid>framboids</framboid>: grains of pyrite that crystallize in those husk piles and warm their water as they burn out over a few minutes. So, a die-off leaves a warm oasis behind it for a while. Heat spreads a bit in the water, is distributed by the currents, and dissipates toward the climate's <water>background</water> temperature within about half a minute. Stone holds heat: reefs and sand warm and cool slowly.
guide.heat.p2: Each species prefers a temperature (its <optimum>optimum</optimum>) and can only stand temperatures a bit above and below that (its <tolerance>tolerance</tolerance>). How well the cell <thermal>works</thermal> falls off slowly in the cold and steeply in the heat, and narrow specialists work best of all at their optimum, so small differences in warmth matter. Swimmers steer toward water that suits them (<thermotaxis>thermotaxis</thermotaxis>). Far too cold, a cell goes <torpor>torpid</torpor>; far too hot, it bleaches and may <scalding>scald</scalding>.
guide.pool.drought: Drought. The water falls until much of the floor lies dry and the pool parts into separate pools. Cells get stranded in the mud as the waterline recedes. The mud pales and cracks into plates as it dries. Eventually, rain falls, staining the mud dark drop by drop until it is wet all over, refills the pool, and the resting cells that survived awake again.
guide.pool.storm: Storm. Cold rain under cloud. Raindrops ripple the surface, bending the view of what lies beneath, and shove the water and what floats in it.
guide.pool.duckweed: Duckweed. A few fronds of duckweed float out of focus far above, a mother and the daughters budding from it, drifting slowly and shading the water under them. Each hangs a root down through the water.
guide.pool.frost: Frost. A cold night chills the water to near 0° and ice grows over the pool as a mass of small crystals, pushing cells into the veins of water between ice sheets. Eventually, the ice thaws, and the torpid cells that survived being trapped in the ice awake again.
guide.pool.p2: Cells stranded on dry mud or caught in ice cannot swim or feed. They show <cystdry>dried or frozen</cystdry>; most rest as <cyst>cysts</cyst> and wait, losing energy very slowly, and the rest starve. The water's edge pulls cells near it back in. After each event the log tallies how much life and how many species were lost. Rain wakes cysts fast, so a drought ends in a burst of hatching.
guide.pool.p3: Settings → Climate allows turning all events off, or toggling each kind event separately. It also has an option to immediately start a new event of any type.
guide.cells.p3: When a cell divides, a developmental rule picks the child’s type from the parent’s type. That rule produces the <bodyplan>body plan</bodyplan>, for example α 60 · β 40.
guide.cells.p4: Species with <adhesion>adhesion</adhesion> form <bond>bonds</bond>: each cell keeps up to two partners of the same species. New bonds fill empty slots with nearby cells, and children start bonded to their parent, so bodies grow by division. A bond lasts until a partner dies, changes kind, or stretches too far away. Bonds are rendered by curving link lines, so a web of links is one <organism>organism</organism>. Species without adhesion are single-celled and never show links, however closely they crowd.
guide.movement.pairwise-forces: Pushes and pulls from everything within its reach: another living cell that comes inside its personal space is shoved away; anything further out draws it closer or pushes it off, depending on how attracted it is to that kind of thing, most strongly at middle distance. Its thrust sets how hard it responds.
guide.movement.phototaxis: Phototaxis: in species that have it, a push towards the light (or away from it).
guide.movement.currents: Currents, the water itself pushing the cell scaled by current pull.
guide.movement.p2: There is no pathfinding and no sense beyond about 60 µm, except for which way the light and the warmth grow. Roamers are swimmers that travel until forces bend their path. Self-propelled bodies come from chases between cell types: if β is drawn to α while α pushes β away, β chases α forever and the body drives itself forward. Evolution keeps whichever pulls lead to food.
guide.ecology.p1: Producers are photosynthetic cells, usually anchored colonies and free-floating drifters. Consumers are grazers that crop producers. Scavengers consume husks and dung. And, predators hunt the grazers and scavengers. Every world founds at least two species in each of these niches. Several pressures shape which forms thrive:
guide.ecology.fleeing: Prey <flee>flee</flee> their hunters and hide among dense producers. Well-fed hunters rest (<satiety>satiety</satiety>), so they do not eat each other to death.
guide.ecology.catching: Catching takes skill: cells catch living prey in proportion to how well they are built to eat it, so producers and husk eaters rarely kill other animal cells.
guide.ecology.currents: Anchored producers thrive where currents run strong; drifting ones where they are calm. Bonded bodies live cheaply and resist attack but disperse poorly.
guide.ecology.climate: The climate keeps changing which strategy wins as the temperature shifts, so dominant species trade places as those more tuned to the current climate prosper.
guide.evolution.p1: Every mutant creates a new <species>species</species>. Mutations nudge every gene: signatures, diet, swimming, adhesion, color and more. Occasionally a whole cell type is reinvented or copied over another. Most mutants vanish within seconds; those that reach the population threshold become <thriving>thriving</thriving> and are named.
guide.reading.census: Census: the bar splits every particle between living cells, husks, stone and silt. The chart below it stacks living cells by species in their colors (point at a band to show the species name, click to highlight it); the pale top band is life in species too small to list, and dotted lines mark new eras.
guide.reading.scale: Scale: the ticks above the controls are round lengths in micrometers (or millimeters, when zoomed out); the scale legend at the bottom right says how long.
guide.tools.specimen: Specimen (click or tap a particle): a live close-up, its energy and age, its behavior, its body, its species and its full genome, the record of the selection (its organism traced through its bonds, highlighted and followed as a whole, even after the cell you picked dies).
guide.tools.lab-species: Lab → Species: every species, filtered by status, diet, movement, and body. Highlight these dims everything outside the filter.
guide.tools.lab-lineage: Lab → Lineage: the family trees of the most successful species. A lineage is a line of descent, followed through every species it evolves into. The top shows each lineage’s cells over time, with every branch drawn inside the lineage it came from, so a die-off shows as the whole stack falling. The tree below lists the same lineages, each with a species count. Click a row or a band to explore that lineage, or drag across the plot to zoom into a stretch of time. Smaller branches appear as you zoom in, down to single species. Point at a row and click its reticle to see where that species is in the water. A zoomed time range shows beside it, and × resets it. Esc or Backspace goes back one step.
guide.tools.lab-census: Lab → Census (the Field Lab's first section, the column on the left; fold it away by clicking the header or pressing K): the world broken down by matter, diet, movement, body, cell type and condition, the chart of living cells by species, and the latest log entries. Choose a row to highlight it in the world.
guide.tools.lab-charts: Lab → Charts: population, diversity, births, deaths, meals, climate over time, and the eras so far.
guide.tools.lab-log: Lab → Log: every logged event, searchable. The chronicler’s stories, written now and then when something notable has happened, show in a warmer color.
guide.tools.card: Card (in the specimen panel): a species card to save and share. You can also name the species in the card view.
guide.tools.film: Film (R): records the view as a video, captions and soundtrack included, until you stop it (R again).
guide.tools.auto: Auto: the camera drifts around the world on its own, with captions saying what it is showing. It will activate automatically after a minute of idle time (can be switched off in Settings).
